sections.title: DISCUSSION
sections.text:
Issued at 133 AM EDT Thu Sep 24 2026

The bottom end of the upper trough will be swinging over the 
southern Appalachians today on its way to its rendezvous with the 
coastal storm. This should help initiate some additional rain 
showers, mainly in the morning hours but cannot rule out an isolated 
shower in the afternoon. Cannot rule out thunder with today's 
activity, but if any bark occurs not expecting a bite. Next few 
mornings starting Friday morning will be pleasantly cool, and a few 
lucky souls in southwest VA or far northeastern TN may see 
temperatures dip below 40F! For example, there's a 30% chance of 
this occurring per the NBM at both Mountain City and Glade Spring. 

Trough quickly ejects offshore as we head into the weekend and 
backside flow means we should be dry, pleasantly warm but 
comfortable with low afternoon RH values, and enjoying a good 
entrance into normal early fall weather for the MidSouth. Rain 
chances don't look to return until next Wednesday when both major 
models agree that a classic fall longwave trough will march from 
west to east across the CONUS. GFS is doing its usual too speedy 
bias, but NBM increases rain chances Wednesday to end the forecast 
and the month of September.

&&

sections.title: AVIATION
sections.text:
(06Z TAFS)
Issued at 133 AM EDT Thu Sep 24 2026

Shower chances will taper off shortly after issuance with sites
varying from VFR to IFR cigs. Most sites should transition to
solid MVFR as low stratus builds in overnight. Brief stints at IFR
is likely, but doubtful to prevail. Some fog may develop, but
light winds should keep some mixing and limit it. A slow return to
VFR as cigs gradually increase and scatter by mid-afternoon
Thursday. A non-zero chance for some additional showers around
daybreak and opted for a PROB30 at TYS.

enso.title: ENSO Alert System Status: El Niño Advisory
paragraphs: ENSO Alert System Status: El Niño Advisory Synopsis: El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026-27. El Niño strengthened further over the past month, with sea surface temperature anomalies exceeding +3.0°C in the eastern equatorial Pacific [Fig. 1] . Except for the Niño-4 index, which decreased to +0.1°C in August, values in the other Niño indices increased, reaching +1.8°C in Niño-3.4, +2.5°C in Niño-3, and +3.4°C in Niño-1+2 [Fig. 2] . The equatorial subsurface temperature index (average from 180°-100°W) remained steady during August [Fig. 3] , reflecting a deeper-than-average thermocline [Fig. 4] . Subsurface temperatures continued to be significantly above average, with widespread anomalies in excess of +10.0°C at depth. Low-level westerly wind anomalies and upper-level easterly wind anomalies extended from the western to the east-central equatorial Pacific. Enhanced convection and rainfall persisted from the central to the eastern Pacific, while anomalies remained suppressed over Indonesia [Fig. 5] . The traditional and equatorial Southern Oscillation indices remained negative. Collectively, the coupled ocean-atmosphere system reflected a strengthening El Niño. The CPC Official ENSO outlook , which synthesizes multiple models from North America and abroad, indicates El Niño will continue to strengthen through the end of the year [Figs. 6

-8] . During the October-December 2026 season, there is a 75% chance of a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950 (+2.5°C or more for a 3-month RONI value ). With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Niño are larger, though not guaranteed (see CPC outlooks for probabilities of seasonal anomalies). In summary, El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026-27. This discussion is a consolidated effort of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), NOAA's National Weather Service, and their funded institutions. md.summary: Isolated strong thunderstorm development posing at least a risk for severe hail appears increasingly probable by 4-6 PM MDT. This may be maintained for a couple of hours late this afternoon into evening. Although this is still not anticipated to require a severe weather watch, trends will be monitored.
md.discussion: Stronger boundary-layer warming and deeper mixing has become focused near a weak surface low across the southeastern Montana/western Dakotas border vicinity, with some north-northeastward development still possible through late afternoon. Near the interface of this environment, and a narrow corridor of better low-level moisture return to the north/east, it appears that boundary-layer destabilization may maximize around the Dickinson, ND vicinity by 22-00Z. Aided by lift associated with a corresponding focused area of stronger low-level warm advection, as low-amplitude mid-level troughing continues to overspread the region, it appears that thunderstorms will initiate as remaining inhibition erodes. Near and just to the northwest of a strong southwesterly mid/upper jet (including speeds on the order of 40-70 kt in the 500-700 mb layer), updraft inflow of boundary-layer air characterized by CAPE up to 1000+ J/kg may support an evolving supercell structure. As this tends to propagate eastward, or east-southeastward, it may pose primarily a risk for severe hail, with perhaps some potential for locally damaging surface gusts and/or a brief tornado, for at least a couple of hours late this afternoon into evening.
